questions.question: Clearance is best defined as the:
options: A. Time for the level to halve
B. Volume of plasma cleared per unit time
C. Total drug amount in the body
D. Fraction of the dose absorbed
questions.explanation: Clearance is the plasma volume completely cleared of drug per unit time; it sets the maintenance dose.

questions.question: With regular dosing, steady state is reached after roughly how many half-lives?
questions.explanation: Steady state (rate in = rate out) is reached after 3-5 half-lives, independent of the dose size.

questions.question: Which drugs are poorly excreted renally because they are passively reabsorbed?
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble drugs diffuse back out of the tubule with reabsorbed water, so they are not efficiently excreted - the reason metabolism exists.

questions.question: A classic example of genetic variation in metabolism is the existence of:
questions.explanation: Genetic polymorphisms (e.g. slow vs fast acetylators) can profoundly change drug levels between individuals.

questions.question: The enterohepatic circulation tends to do what to a drug's action?
questions.explanation: Bile secretes drug to the gut where it is reabsorbed and recirculates, prolonging the drug's stay and effect.

questions.question: Why must lipid-soluble drugs be metabolised before the kidney can excrete them?
options: A. They are too small to filter
B. They are passively reabsorbed with water
C. They bind irreversibly to OATs
D. They cannot enter the tubule
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble drugs filtered at the glomerulus are reabsorbed back with water; metabolism makes them water-soluble so they stay in the urine.

questions.question: In first-order elimination, what is removed per unit time?
questions.explanation: First-order removes a constant fraction (percentage) per unit time; rate is proportional to concentration and clearance is constant.

questions.question: In zero-order kinetics, as concentration rises the clearance:
options: B. Falls (a fixed amount is removed)
questions.explanation: Once pathways saturate, a fixed amount is removed per unit time, so clearance falls as concentration climbs - small dose rises can be toxic.

questions.question: The elimination rate constant (kel) relates to half-life by which expression?
questions.explanation: kel = 0.693 / t1/2 (0.693 = ln2); it is the fraction of drug eliminated per unit time. Also CL = kel x Vd.

questions.question: Probenecid raises and prolongs penicillin levels by:
options: D. Sharply raising the urine pH
questions.explanation: Probenecid inhibits the organic anion transporter (OAT) that secretes penicillin into the tubule, slowing its excretion.

questions.question: In active tubular secretion, basic (protonated) drugs are carried by which transporters?
questions.explanation: OCTs carry basic (cationic) drugs; OATs carry acidic (anionic) drugs into the tubule.

questions.question: Which set of CYP enzymes accounts for over half of small-molecule drug metabolism?
questions.explanation: CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6 and 3A4 handle over 50% of small-molecule metabolism; 3A4 is the busiest.

questions.question: S-warfarin is more potent than R-warfarin and is metabolised mainly by:
questions.explanation: S-warfarin (the more potent enantiomer) is metabolised by CYP2C9, so a CYP2C9 inhibitor raises the potent isomer selectively.

questions.question: For the 25-30% of drugs excreted mainly unchanged (active), renal impairment causes:
questions.explanation: Drugs cleared mainly as unchanged active drug accumulate when renal function falls, raising toxicity risk.

questions.question: A very large volume of distribution (Vd) indicates that the drug is:
questions.explanation: A large Vd means the drug leaves the plasma into tissues (low plasma concentration for the dose); minimal tissue binding gives a Vd near plasma volume.

shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PII · Shoulder Region
shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.content: L2 Anatomy of the shoulder region: bones, joints, muscles and rotator cuff.

questions.question: Which two bones form the pectoral girdle?
questions.explanation: The pectoral girdle is an incomplete ring of the clavicle and scapula, slinging the limb onto the trunk.

questions.question: Viewed from above, the clavicle has what shape?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is doubly curved - an elongated 'S' - with the medial two-thirds convex and lateral third concave.

questions.question: What are the three processes of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The scapula's three processes are the coracoid, the acromion and the spine (learn it as 2 surfaces, 2 angles, 3 borders, 3 processes).

questions.question: The shallow glenoid cavity is deepened by which structure?
questions.explanation: The fibrocartilage glenoid labrum deepens the shallow socket; the rotator cuff then actively holds the head in.

questions.question: Which three joints make up the shoulder region?
questions.explanation: The sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular and glenohumeral joints - described by surfaces, ligaments, class and movements.

questions.question: What structural class is the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint?
questions.explanation: It is a ball-and-socket synovial joint - the most mobile in the body, at the cost of stability.

questions.question: The rotator cuff muscles are remembered by which acronym?
questions.explanation: SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the deltoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid (and teres minor); it winds around the surgical neck of the humerus.

questions.question: The sternal (medial) end of the clavicle articulates with which bone?
options: A. The acromion of the scapula
B. The manubrium of the sternum
questions.explanation: The triangular sternal end meets the manubrium (and 1st costal cartilage) at the sternoclavicular joint - the girdle's only axial link.

questions.question: The supraglenoid tubercle is the origin of which muscle head?
questions.explanation: The supraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the long head of biceps; the infraglenoid tubercle gives the long head of triceps.

questions.question: What does the articular disc of the sternoclavicular joint do?
options: A. It removes the need for ligaments
B. It splits the joint cavity into two
C. It converts it into a hinge joint
D. It blocks nearly all movement
questions.explanation: The disc splits the SC cavity into two compartments and bonds to all the ligaments - the reason the joint is so strong.

questions.question: Which ligament provides the main weight-bearing stability of the AC joint?
questions.explanation: The extrinsic coracoclavicular ligament (trapezoid + conoid bands) slings the scapula from the clavicle and bears the limb's weight.

questions.question: What is the specific action of supraspinatus at the shoulder?
options: B. Starts the first 15 degrees of abduction
D. Only medially rotates the arm
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates the first ~15 degrees of abduction and pulls the head into the glenoid; deltoid takes over beyond that.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior; injury causes a winged scapula.

questions.question: Which nerve provides the motor supply to trapezius?
questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is the motor supply; C3/C4 carry sensation. Superior/middle/inferior fibres elevate/retract/depress.

questions.question: Which rotator-cuff muscle inserts on the LESSER tubercle of the humerus?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis (the only anterior cuff muscle) inserts on the lesser tubercle; the other three (S/I/T) insert on the greater tubercle.

questions.question: Why are clavicle fractures common while sternoclavicular dislocations are rare?
options: A. The clavicle has no supporting ligaments
B. The disc binds the SC ligaments, making it strong
C. The clavicle carries no body weight
D. The SC joint has no joint capsule
questions.explanation: The articular disc is fixed to all the SC ligaments, making the joint extremely strong, so force fractures the bone before dislocating the joint.

questions.question: In which direction does the shoulder usually dislocate, and which nerve is at risk?
questions.explanation: The capsule is weakest antero-inferiorly and the arch blocks superior escape, so dislocation is antero-inferior ('pointed shoulder'); the axillary nerve is at risk.

questions.question: In the 'lady between two majors', which muscle attaches to the FLOOR of the bicipital groove?
questions.explanation: Latissimus dorsi (the 'LADY') is in the floor; pectoralis major takes the lateral lip and teres major the medial lip.

questions.question: What is the approximate glenohumeral-to-scapular ratio of shoulder abduction?
questions.explanation: About 2:1 - roughly 2 degrees at the glenohumeral joint per 1 degree of scapular rotation (~120 GH + ~60 scapular for ~180 total).

questions.question: A winged scapula results from paralysis of which muscle/nerve?
options: B. Serratus anterior / long thoracic nerve
questions.explanation: Serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) holds the scapula to the chest wall; its palsy lets the medial border lift off - a winged scapula.

questions.question: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus are both supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; subscapularis is supplied by the subscapular nerves and teres minor by the axillary nerve.

questions.question: The coraco-acromial arch protects the head but predisposes to which problem?
options: C. Dislocation of the elbow joint
D. Winging of the scapula on pushing
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa pass through the narrow space under the arch, so they get pinched - subacromial impingement.

questions.question: Which nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and is at risk in a fracture there?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve (with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels) wraps the surgical neck; a fracture there can paralyse deltoid and numb the 'regimental badge' area.

bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W3 PII · Bone Physiology II
bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.content: Bone fracture healing cascade, callus formation, remodelling, malunion and nonunion.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the four fracture-healing stages?
options: A. Haematoma, soft callus, bony callus, remodelling
B. Soft callus, haematoma, remodelling, bony callus
C. Bony callus, haematoma, soft callus, remodelling
D. Remodelling, haematoma, soft callus, bony callus
questions.explanation: Healing runs haematoma (0-1 days), fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, bony (hard) callus, then remodelling (ongoing).

questions.question: Which is the immediate first stage of fracture healing (0-1 days)?
options: A. Formation of the fracture haematoma
B. Formation of the bony (hard) callus
questions.explanation: Torn vessels bleed and clot at the break, forming the fracture haematoma - the scaffold and signal box for repair.

questions.question: Which cells lay down the cartilage of the soft callus?
options: D. Red blood cells in the clot
questions.explanation: Chondroblasts/chondrocytes lay down the cartilage-and-collagen soft callus that bridges the gap before it is replaced by bone.

questions.question: Which cells build the bone matrix of the hard callus?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts lay down bone matrix, converting the soft callus into a bony (hard) callus.

questions.question: During remodelling, which cells resorb the excess bony callus?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb the over-built callus while osteoblasts deposit new bone, reshaping it to the original contour.

questions.question: A defining feature of fracture repair is that bone heals with:
options: B. New bone, not scar tissue
questions.explanation: Unlike most tissues, bone regenerates with bone rather than scar, so a healed fracture can regain full strength.

questions.question: Nonunion is failure of a fracture to heal after about:
questions.explanation: Nonunion is failure to unite after roughly 9 months, usually from lost stability or blood supply.

questions.question: Malunion describes a fracture that has:
options: A. Failed to unite at all
B. Healed in a poor position
questions.explanation: Malunion is union with a change in angle or length (heals crooked); nonunion is failure to unite.

questions.question: Low oxygen (hypoxia) in the fracture haematoma stimulates release of:
questions.explanation: Hypoxia drives VEGF release, which grows new blood vessels (angiogenesis) into the clot - the basis of repair.

questions.question: Which cells are recruited to the fracture and differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts?
questions.explanation: Growth factors recruit mesenchymal stem cells that migrate to and within the fracture, then differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts.

questions.question: During callus formation, 'endochondral ossification' means:
options: A. Bone forming within a membrane
B. Bone replacing a cartilage template
D. Bone being resorbed by osteoclasts
questions.explanation: Endo (inside) + chondral (cartilage) + ossification: the cartilage soft callus is a template converted into bone.

questions.question: Compared with lamellar bone, the woven bone of the callus is:
options: B. Irregular in collagen, fast, weak
C. Only ever found in children
questions.explanation: Woven bone has irregular collagen and is laid down fast but weak; it is later replaced by ordered, load-bearing lamellar bone.

questions.question: Remodelling reshapes the callus along lines of stress according to:
options: A. Starling's law of the heart
B. Wolff's law of bone loading
D. Boyle's law of gas volume
questions.explanation: Wolff's law: bone is deposited where loaded and resorbed where not, restoring contour and strength along stress lines.

questions.question: Primary (direct) bone healing, unlike secondary healing, occurs when:
options: B. Fragments are rigidly fixed, no callus
C. The haematoma is very large
D. Blood supply is completely lost
questions.explanation: Rigid fixation lets bone heal directly across the gap with no visible callus (primary healing); a little movement drives callus (secondary).

questions.question: The fibrin meshwork of the haematoma mainly serves as:
options: A. A calcium store for the cell
B. A scaffold for cell migration
D. A source of new osteoclasts
questions.explanation: The clot's fibrin meshwork is the scaffold cells crawl along to reach and bridge the fracture gap.

questions.question: Which is a MODIFIABLE risk factor for impaired fracture healing?
questions.explanation: Smoking (a vasoconstrictor) is modifiable, as are diabetes control, nutrition and vitamin D; age and fracture pattern are not.

questions.question: Why is restoring blood supply (angiogenesis) the decisive step in healing?
options: A. Cartilage cannot form without vessels
B. Osteoblasts need oxygen to make bone
C. Platelets only work in high oxygen
D. Fibrin requires oxygen to form
questions.explanation: Cartilage tolerates low oxygen but osteoblasts (bone) need oxygen; without new vessels the repair stalls at cartilage or dies, causing nonunion.

questions.question: Which combination is used to treat an established nonunion?
options: A. Rest and simple analgesia only
B. Ultrasound, bone graft/BMP, and fixation
C. A short course of antibiotics
questions.explanation: Nonunion is treated with external stimulation (ultrasound), internal stimulation (bone graft, BMP) and fixation (ORIF).

questions.question: A rare treatment-related complication of BMP used for nonunion is:
options: C. Loss of all bone marrow
questions.explanation: Bone morphogenic protein can rescue a nonunion but rarely causes heterotopic ossification - bone forming where it should not.

questions.question: Within the fracture haematoma, platelets are activated by:
options: A. Vitamin D from the skin
B. Thrombin in the clotting cascade
questions.explanation: Thrombin activates platelets, which release the growth factors that kick off the repair cascade.

questions.question: The usual treatment for a symptomatic malunion is:
options: A. Simple rest and ice packs
questions.explanation: A malunion is corrected by osteotomy (re-cutting the bone) then fixation, e.g. ORIF.

questions.question: The soft callus is converted to hard callus when:
options: B. Osteoblasts replace it with woven bone
C. Fibroblasts lay down scar tissue
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts replace the cartilage template with woven bone (endochondral ossification), forming the bony/hard callus.

questions.question: The two make-or-break requirements for a fracture to unite are:
options: A. Warmth and a large haematoma
B. Stability and a blood supply
C. High movement and low oxygen
questions.explanation: Healing needs stability and blood supply; the risk factors for nonunion all reduce to losing one of these (plus materials/signal).

questions.question: Why can a child's slightly angulated fracture straighten over time?
options: B. Their vigorous remodelling reshapes it
D. The periosteum is absent in children
questions.explanation: Children remodel bone vigorously (Wolff's law), so even a fracture that heals slightly angled can straighten - paediatric fractures are often managed conservatively.

muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W3 PIII · Muscle Physiology I
muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.content: Skeletal muscle structure, neuromuscular junction, sliding filament contraction and relaxation.

questions.question: Which muscle type is striated, multinucleate and under voluntary control?
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate and voluntary; cardiac is striated but involuntary, smooth is non-striated and involuntary.

questions.question: Which connective-tissue sheath surrounds a whole muscle?
questions.explanation: Epimysium wraps the whole muscle, perimysium each fascicle, endomysium each fibre; all merge into the tendon.

questions.question: Which sheath wraps an individual muscle fibre?
questions.explanation: Endomysium wraps each single fibre and carries the capillaries and fine nerve endings.

questions.question: The Z disc anchors which protein and marks which point of the sarcomere?
questions.explanation: The Z disc anchors actin at the edge (boundary) of the sarcomere; the M line anchors myosin in the middle.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation: Somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine (ACh) at the NMJ; its effect on skeletal muscle is always excitatory.

questions.question: The effect of a somatic motor neuron on a skeletal muscle fibre is always:
questions.explanation: Unlike the autonomic system, somatic motor neurons can only excite the fibre (via ACh); relaxation happens when firing stops.

questions.question: Which structure inside the muscle fibre stores calcium for contraction?
questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (modified ER) wraps the myofibrils and stores calcium, releasing it on depolarisation.

questions.question: Which sarcomere region contains myosin only (no actin overlap)?
questions.explanation: The H zone is the central A-band region with myosin only; the I band is actin only; the A band is the overlap.

questions.question: In the sliding-filament theory, during contraction the filaments:
options: D. Detach from the Z discs
questions.explanation: Actin and myosin keep their length and slide past one another; the sarcomere shortens as the Z discs are drawn in.

questions.question: During contraction, which sarcomere band does NOT change width?
questions.explanation: The A band equals the fixed myosin length, so it is unchanged; the I band and H zone narrow as filaments slide together.

questions.question: The nicotinic ACh receptor at the motor end plate is best described as a:
questions.explanation: It is ligand-gated (opened by ACh) and non-specific for cations (passes Na and K).

questions.question: Opening the nicotinic receptor lets Na and K move; the net effect is:
options: C. No change in membrane voltage
questions.explanation: Na influx exceeds K efflux (because of the gradients), so the net inward current depolarises the end plate.

questions.question: At rest, which protein blocks the myosin-binding sites on actin?
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin lies over actin's binding sites at rest; troponin (with calcium) moves it aside to allow contraction.

questions.question: Calcium initiates contraction by binding to which protein?
questions.explanation: Calcium binds troponin, which changes shape and pulls tropomyosin off the binding sites, exposing actin to myosin.

questions.question: What is the main role of the transverse (T) tubules?
options: A. To store and release calcium ions
B. To carry the impulse deep into the fibre
C. To synthesise ATP for contraction
D. To anchor and align the myofibrils
questions.explanation: T-tubules are infoldings of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fibre toward the SR, so it contracts as one.

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is usually treated with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor such as:
questions.explanation: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase, so ACh is broken down more slowly and more is available for the surviving (autoimmune-depleted) receptors.

questions.question: Botulinum toxin produces which effect on muscle?
questions.explanation: Botulinum blocks ACh release from the axon, so no depolarisation occurs - flaccid paralysis (used therapeutically as Botox).

questions.question: Tetanus toxin causes spastic paralysis because it:
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxin blocks inhibitory interneurons in the CNS ('disinhibition'), so motor neurons fire unchecked - spastic paralysis.

questions.question: In excitation-contraction coupling, the T-tubule DHP receptor opens which channel?
options: B. The ryanodine receptor on the SR
questions.explanation: The DHP voltage sensor mechanically opens the ryanodine receptor (RyR) on the SR, releasing calcium into the sarcoplasm.

questions.question: In the cross-bridge cycle, release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) triggers:
questions.explanation: After myosin binds actin, releasing Pi drives the power stroke that pulls actin toward the M line.

questions.question: What actually detaches the myosin head from actin, ending a cross-bridge?
options: B. A fresh ATP binding myosin
questions.explanation: A new ATP binding to myosin breaks the actin-myosin bond; without ATP the head stays bound (the rigor state).

questions.question: Rigor mortis develops after death because:
options: A. Excess ATP is produced after death
B. Calcium leaks in while ATP runs out
D. Myosin dissolves in the sarcoplasm
questions.explanation: The SR leaks calcium (cross-bridges keep forming) while no ATP is made (they cannot detach), so the muscle locks stiff.

questions.question: Excess nicotine at the nicotinic receptor can cause paralysis by:
options: B. Prolonged depolarisation of the plate
D. Pumping calcium into the SR
questions.explanation: Nicotine activates the nAChR; in excess it causes prolonged depolarisation (depolarising block) and, chronically, receptor desensitisation.

questions.question: Calcium is returned to the sarcoplasmic reticulum during relaxation by:
questions.explanation: The SR calcium-ATPase (SERCA) actively pumps calcium back into the store, lowering sarcoplasmic calcium so tropomyosin recovers the binding sites.

questions.question: During the power stroke, the myosin head pulls the actin filament toward the:
options: A. Z disc, ~10 nm per stroke
B. M line, ~10 nm per stroke
D. I band, ~50 nm per stroke
questions.explanation: Each power stroke ratchets actin ~10 nm toward the M line (sarcomere centre); many cycles produce visible shortening.

questions.question: Curariform muscle relaxants are used in anaesthesia because they:
options: B. Block the nAChR, causing relaxation
questions.explanation: Curariform drugs block the nicotinic receptor so the muscle cannot be told to contract - controlled relaxation/paralysis for surgery.

questions.question: Why does muscle relaxation also require ATP, not just contraction?
options: A. ATP is only needed to contract
B. ATP detaches myosin and re-pumps calcium
D. ATP breaks down the actin
questions.explanation: ATP is needed to detach myosin from actin AND to pump calcium back into the SR against its gradient - no ATP means the muscle stays contracted (rigor).

ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.title: MHHS2402 W3 · Ventilation & Gas Exchange
ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.content: Respiratory functions, fluid-movement laws, lung mechanics, volumes and capacities, gas diffusion and V/Q.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the five functions of the respiratory system?
questions.explanation: The five functions are air conduction, conditioning/protection, gas exchange, pH regulation and vocalisation - not digestion.

questions.question: Which part of the airway is air-only (not shared with food)?
questions.explanation: The lower tract (trachea, bronchi, alveoli) carries only air; the pharynx and mouth are shared with food.

questions.question: Surfactant is produced by which cells?
questions.explanation: Alveolar (type II) cells make surfactant, which lines alveoli and small bronchioles (half-life ~14 h).

questions.question: Boyle's law states that pressure and volume of a fixed gas are:
questions.explanation: P is inversely proportional to V (P1V1 = P2V2); expanding the lungs lowers their pressure so air flows in.

questions.question: At rest, the intrapleural pressure is:
questions.explanation: Intrapleural pressure is negative; pleural-fluid cohesion makes the elastic lung follow the chest wall.

questions.question: The main muscle of inspiration is the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm contracts and flattens downward to enlarge the thorax; external intercostals and scalenes assist.

questions.question: An adult's tidal volume is approximately:
questions.explanation: Tidal volume (one normal breath) is around 0.5 L.

questions.question: Vital capacity is the sum of which volumes?
questions.explanation: Vital capacity = tidal + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve (all the air you can move); total lung capacity adds residual volume.

questions.question: Gas exchange between air and blood occurs mainly at the:
questions.explanation: Exchange happens at the alveoli, which have the largest total cross-sectional area and lowest resistance.

questions.question: Gas exchange across the alveolar membrane is driven mainly by:
questions.explanation: Gases diffuse down their partial-pressure gradients; in healthy lungs this difference is the dominant factor.

questions.question: The ventilation-perfusion ratio (V/Q) is defined as:
questions.explanation: V/Q = alveolar ventilation / blood flow; it measures how well air and blood are matched for exchange.

questions.question: The normal whole-lung ventilation-perfusion ratio is about:
questions.explanation: Normal V/Q is about 0.8 (roughly 4 L/min ventilation over 5 L/min cardiac output).

questions.question: Surfactant improves alveolar stability by:
options: A. Raising surface tension a lot
B. Reducing surface tension, most at low volumes
questions.explanation: Surfactant lowers surface tension - more at low volumes - so small alveoli do not collapse into larger ones.

questions.question: By Laplace's law (P = 2T/r), a smaller alveolus needs:
options: A. A lower pressure to stay open
B. A higher pressure to stay open
D. The same pressure as a large one
questions.explanation: For a fixed surface tension, a smaller radius needs a higher pressure to stay open, so small alveoli tend to empty into larger ones without surfactant.

questions.question: Airway resistance depends most dramatically on which variable?
options: B. Radius to the fourth power
questions.explanation: By Poiseuille's law R = 8uL/(pi r^4); resistance depends on radius to the fourth power, so small narrowing collapses flow.

questions.question: During inspiration the diaphragm:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm contracts and flattens down, enlarging the thorax so intrapleural and alveolar pressure fall and air flows in.

questions.question: Which volume CANNOT be measured by simple spirometry?
questions.explanation: Residual volume is the air that cannot be exhaled, so it never crosses the spirometer; capacities containing it need indirect methods.

questions.question: Minute ventilation is calculated as:
options: B. Tidal volume x respiratory rate
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation (V-dot) = tidal volume x respiratory rate; it matters more than either value alone.

questions.question: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the sum of which volumes?
questions.explanation: FRC = expiratory reserve volume + residual volume (the air left after a normal breath out).

questions.question: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which dissociates into:
questions.explanation: CO2 + H2O gives H2CO3, which yields H+ and HCO3-; more CO2 means more H+ (lower pH), so ventilation tunes blood pH.

questions.question: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals:
options: B. The sum of the partial pressures
questions.explanation: Total pressure is the sum of the individual (partial) pressures; each gas diffuses down its own partial-pressure gradient.

questions.question: Applying Boyle's law to inspiration, increasing lung volume:
options: A. Raises lung pressure above atmospheric
B. Lowers lung pressure below atmospheric
questions.explanation: Bigger volume means lower pressure; when lung pressure drops below atmospheric, air flows in.

questions.question: Forced (active) expiration is assisted by which muscles?
options: D. No muscles - it is passive
questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil; forced expiration adds the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals.

questions.question: Bulk flow (unlike diffusion) refers to movement of:
options: A. A single gas down a gradient
B. The whole air mixture together
questions.explanation: Bulk flow moves the entire air mixture into/out of the lungs; diffusion moves individual gases across the membrane.

questions.question: Halving the radius of an airway changes its resistance by a factor of about:
questions.explanation: Resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, so halving the radius raises resistance 16-fold (2^4) - why small narrowing chokes flow in asthma.

questions.question: Why is the negative intrapleural pressure essential for breathing?
options: A. It actively powers the diaphragm
B. It holds the lung to the chest wall
C. It warms and humidifies air
questions.explanation: Lung tissue has no muscle; the negative intrapleural pressure (via pleural-fluid cohesion) keeps it expanded against the chest wall - losing it causes pneumothorax.

questions.question: A ventilation-perfusion ratio of zero (V/Q = 0) represents:
options: B. A shunt: perfused, not ventilated
questions.explanation: V/Q = 0 means an alveolus is perfused but not ventilated (a shunt); blood passes without being oxygenated.

questions.question: A ventilation-perfusion ratio approaching infinity represents:
options: B. Dead space: ventilated, not perfused
questions.explanation: V/Q approaching infinity means ventilation without perfusion (dead space), classically a pulmonary embolism.

questions.question: In the Fick diffusion relationship, rate is proportional to the partial-pressure difference and area, and inversely to:
questions.explanation: Diffusion rate ~ (dP x area x solubility)/(distance x sqrt(MW)); a thicker membrane (greater distance) slows diffusion.

questions.question: Emphysema impairs gas diffusion mainly by:
questions.explanation: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing surface area (A) for diffusion; fibrosis/oedema instead increase membrane distance.

questions.question: Pulmonary fibrosis or oedema impairs diffusion by:
questions.explanation: Fibrosis/oedema thicken the alveolar-capillary membrane, increasing the distance (d) gases must cross.

questions.question: Humid alveolar air has a slightly lower pO2 than dry air because:
options: A. Oxygen is destroyed in the lung
B. Water vapour takes part of the pressure
questions.explanation: Water vapour (~47 mmHg) claims part of the total pressure, so pO2 in humid lung air (~150-155) is below dry air (~160 mmHg).

questions.question: A LOW ventilation-perfusion ratio is typically seen in:
options: D. Total loss of lung perfusion
questions.explanation: Low V/Q means poor ventilation (or high perfusion): asthma, chronic bronchitis and acute pulmonary oedema.

questions.question: A HIGH ventilation-perfusion ratio is typically seen in:
questions.explanation: High V/Q means poor perfusion (PE) or high ventilation to compensate (emphysema).

questions.question: In the oxygen cascade, oxygen flows down partial-pressure gradients from the atmosphere ultimately to the:
questions.explanation: O2 descends a cascade atmosphere to alveolus to blood to tissues to mitochondria (the lowest pO2, where it is used).

questions.question: Which capacity includes the residual volume, so it cannot be measured by spirometry alone?
questions.explanation: FRC (and total lung capacity) include residual volume, which spirometry cannot measure - indirect methods (helium dilution) are needed.

respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.title: MHHS2402 W4 · Respiratory Regulation Inputs
respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.content: Respiratory regulation = a homeostatic negative-feedback loop: change (stimulus) -> detector (sensor) -> processing centre -> effector (action on minute ventilation). Homeostasis is dynamic balance, not rest. You don't breathe because you 'think' you should; a detected physical/chemical change must occur. Negative feedback opposes the change (stabilises); positive feedback amplifies it (e.g. a viral post). Three regulated arterial parameters: O2, CO2, pH (pH tracks CO2). Gas moves high->low partial pressure. Carbonic anhydrase: CO2+H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-; rising CO2 lowers pH. CO2 carried dissolved, as bicarbonate, and as carbaminohaemoglobin; O2 carried Hb-bound and dissolved. Normal arterial: paO2 80-100 mmHg, SaO2 95-99%, paCO2 35-45 mmHg, pH 7.35-7.45, HCO3- 22-26 mEq/L; pH<7.35 acidosis, >7.45 alkalosis (respiratory or metabolic). Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid + aortic bodies, fed ~20x their weight in blood/min so sample arterial blood; sense O2, CO2, H+; the main O2 sensor. O2 response flat until PO2 below normal then steep (hypoxic drive); CO2 response steep/linear; low PO2 and low pH raise CO2 sensitivity; peripheral respond to CO2 ~7x stronger and 5x faster than central. Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H+; H+ can't cross the blood-brain barrier but CO2 can (forms H+ in CSF) -> sensitive to blood CO2, not blood H+ or O2. Reflexes: Hering-Breuer (bronchial stretch receptors via vagus cease inspiration, only at hyperinflation >~3x TV); apnoea (central loss of pacing / physical soft-palate / reflex via J receptors); J (juxtacapillary) receptors in alveolar wall -> apnoea (congestion, pneumonia, histamine, serotonin). Five receptors raise ventilation: irritant (also bronchospasm), proprioceptors (immediate feed-forward in exercise), metaboreceptors (local muscle metabolites CO2/H+/lactate), thermoreceptors, pain. Cough (larynx/trachea/bronchi, vagal, glottis closed, intrapleural >100 mmHg, air out up to 160 km/h), sneeze (nasal), deglutition apnoea. Hyperventilation = excess CO2 loss (hypocapnia), not just fast breathing. Respiratory centre: minute ventilation = rate x tidal volume. DRG generates pacemaker + inspiratory ramp and receives glossopharyngeal input; VRG silent at rest, drives forced breathing; pontine pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration and raises rate; apneustic centre deepens inspiration. Transection: sever pons -> lose smooth rhythm but still breathe; sever medulla -> no breathing (medulla = obligatory generator). Inputs: higher brain, peripheral chemoreceptors (glossopharyngeal), central chemoreceptors, sensory reflexes. Outputs: phrenic nerve (diaphragm), intercostal nerves (intercostals). Communicate any change as: change -> detected how -> processed how -> output where -> action.

questions.question: Homeostasis is best described as:
options: A. Keeping the body completely at rest and unchanging
B. Dynamic balance holding a variable near its optimum
C. Maximising a variable such as blood oxygen
D. A process active only during illness
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is dynamic balance — variables are held near an optimum through constant change, not by being at rest.

questions.question: Which sequence lists the four parts of a homeostatic control loop?
questions.explanation: A loop needs a change (stimulus), a detector (sensor), a processing centre, then an effector action.

questions.question: In the control of breathing, negative feedback:
options: A. Amplifies the initial change in minute ventilation
B. Opposes the change, returning ventilation toward normal
C. Has no effect on minute ventilation
D. Acts only on tidal volume, never rate
questions.explanation: Negative feedback detects a deviation and feeds back a signal that opposes it, stabilising minute ventilation.

questions.question: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?
options: A. A thermostat switching the heater off as a room warms
B. Ventilation rising then being brought back down
C. A social-media post becoming more viral with each re-post
D. Sweating to bring a high body temperature down
questions.explanation: Positive feedback amplifies the initial change — a viral post drives still more re-posts. The others are stabilising (negative) feedback.

questions.question: The three arterial parameters used to regulate ventilation are:
options: A. Oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH
C. Carbon dioxide, bicarbonate and sodium
questions.explanation: The regulated variables are O2, CO2 and pH — and pH largely tracks CO2.

questions.question: A gas diffuses across a membrane from an area of:
options: A. Low to high partial pressure
B. High to low partial pressure
D. High to low, only if it is oxygen
questions.explanation: Gas always moves down its partial-pressure gradient, high to low — ventilation exists to keep those gradients favourable.

questions.question: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses which reaction?
options: A. CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−
questions.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ H+ + bicarbonate — the link between CO2 and pH.

questions.question: A rise in dissolved blood CO2 will:
options: D. Raise pH then lower it
questions.explanation: More CO2 pushes the carbonic-anhydrase reaction right, generating H+ and lowering pH — CO2 and pH are two readings of one thing.

questions.question: The normal arterial PCO2 range is:
questions.explanation: Normal paCO2 is 35–45 mmHg. 80–100 is paO2, 22–26 is bicarbonate (mEq/L), and 7.35–7.45 is pH.

questions.question: An arterial pH of 7.30 indicates:
questions.explanation: pH below 7.35 is acidosis; above 7.45 is alkalosis. Each can be respiratory or metabolic in origin.

questions.question: The peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the:
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors sit in the carotid bodies (carotid bifurcation) and aortic bodies (aortic arch).

questions.question: The body's main oxygen sensor is the:
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors are the main O2 sensor; central chemoreceptors are not particularly sensitive to O2.

questions.question: Because each carotid body receives ~20× its own weight in blood per minute, it effectively samples:
questions.explanation: The huge flow means the sampled blood is essentially arterial — a true read-out of what is delivered to the body.

questions.question: The ventilatory response to O2 rises steeply when:
options: A. Arterial PO2 rises above normal
B. Arterial PO2 falls below normal
C. Arterial PO2 is in the normal range
questions.explanation: The O2 curve is nearly flat across normal and high PO2, and climbs steeply only once PO2 falls below normal (the hypoxic drive).

questions.question: Central chemoreceptors are directly sensitive to:
options: A. Hydrogen ions in the cerebrospinal fluid
B. Hydrogen ions in the blood
D. Blood CO2 acting directly on them
questions.explanation: Central chemoreceptors detect CSF H+. They respond to blood CO2 only indirectly, once it crosses into the CSF and forms H+.

questions.question: Why do central chemoreceptors respond to blood CO2 but not to blood H+?
options: A. They have no receptors for H+
B. Blood H+ is too dilute to matter
C. H+ cannot cross the blood–brain barrier, but CO2 can
questions.explanation: The lipid blood–brain barrier blocks charged H+ but lets uncharged CO2 through; CO2 then forms H+ in the CSF, which is sensed.

questions.question: Compared with central chemoreceptors, peripheral chemoreceptors respond to CO2 roughly:
options: A. 7× more strongly and 5× more rapidly
B. 5× more strongly and 7× more rapidly
C. 2× more strongly and 2× more rapidly
D. Equally strongly but more slowly
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors are about 7× more sensitive and 5× faster than central ones — the rapid-alarm system for CO2.

questions.question: The Hering–Breuer reflex is driven by which receptors?
options: A. Stretch receptors in the bronchi and bronchioles
B. Irritant receptors in the epithelium
questions.explanation: Stretch receptors in the bronchi/bronchioles signal via the vagus to cease inspiration.

questions.question: The Hering–Breuer reflex normally acts only during:
questions.explanation: It is a protective backstop against over-inflation, triggered only at hyperinflation (>~3× normal tidal volume), so it stays silent in quiet breathing.

questions.question: Stimulation of the juxtacapillary (J) receptors in the alveolar wall causes:
options: D. A rise in tidal volume only
questions.explanation: J receptors produce apnoea; they are stimulated by pulmonary congestion, pneumonia, histamine and serotonin.

questions.question: Which receptor produces the immediate rise in ventilation at the start of exercise, before blood gases change?
questions.explanation: Proprioceptors fire with movement itself, driving a feed-forward rise in ventilation that anticipates demand.

questions.question: Metaboreceptors differ from chemoreceptors in that they sense:
options: C. Local metabolite levels within muscle
questions.explanation: Metaboreceptors sense local muscle metabolites (CO2, H+, lactate), not circulating blood gases as chemoreceptors do.

questions.question: During a cough, intrapleural pressure rises above approximately:
questions.explanation: Expiration against a closed glottis drives intrapleural pressure above 100 mmHg; when the glottis opens, air blasts out at up to 160 km/h.

questions.question: Minute ventilation equals:
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation = rate × tidal volume — the only output the respiratory centre can change.

questions.question: Which group generates the basic pacemaker and the inspiratory ramp?
questions.explanation: The DRG generates the pacemaker and inspiratory ramp and is the input site for glossopharyngeal (peripheral chemoreceptor) signals.

questions.question: The ventral respiratory group (VRG) is best described as:
options: A. The main driver of quiet resting breathing
B. Inactive at rest, recruited for forced breathing
questions.explanation: The VRG is inactive in normal quiet breathing and contributes to forced inspiration and expiration when demand rises.

questions.question: If the brainstem is severed between the pons and the medulla, breathing:
options: B. Continues but loses its smooth rhythm
questions.explanation: Removing the pons leaves the medullary generator intact, so breathing continues but the smooth rhythm is lost. Severing the medulla stops breathing entirely.

questions.question: The motor output of the respiratory centre travels via the:
options: B. Phrenic nerve (diaphragm) and intercostal nerves (intercostals)
questions.explanation: Somatic motor output runs in the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm and the intercostal nerves to the intercostal muscles. The glossopharyngeal is an input nerve.

questions.question: Which chain correctly frames any change in breathing?
options: A. Change → detected → processed → output → action
B. Action → output → processed → detected → change
C. Detected → processed → change → action → output
D. Change → action → detected → output → processed
questions.explanation: Every regulatory response can be written as change → how detected → how processed → where output → action (a change in rate and/or tidal volume).

questions.question: In the walking example, the first detector engaged is the:
options: A. Peripheral chemoreceptor sensing low O2
questions.explanation: Movement stimulates proprioceptors before blood O2 falls — a feed-forward response that raises ventilation ahead of demand.

muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W4 · Muscle Physiology II — Tension & Performance
muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.content: Muscle Physiology II (Dr Linda Ban): energy, tension and fibre types. ATP is spent by myosin ATPase (contraction/cross-bridges), Ca-ATPase (relaxation, returns Ca to SR) and Na-K-ATPase (rest, restores ion gradients). Three energy systems: (1) phosphagen/PCr — creatine kinase shuttles phosphate; at rest stores it on creatine as phosphocreatine, during activity regenerates ATP fast (1 ATP/PCr, ~15 s, no O2, rate 4 mol/min, fastest); (2) anaerobic glycolysis — cytoplasm, glucose/glycogen, 2 ATP + pyruvate (rate 2.5), pyruvate becomes lactic acid without O2; (3) aerobic/oxidative phosphorylation — mitochondria, glucose + fatty acids, ~32 ATP + heat (rate 1, slowest, most efficient), O2 from myoglobin + haemoglobin. Speed-vs-yield trade-off, handed off sprint->jog->marathon. Fatigue = muscle can no longer generate/sustain power; depletion (glycogen/O2) and accumulation (lactate, low pH impairing CK/ATPases and Ca-troponin) theories, associative not causal. Recovery repays oxygen debt: alactacid (aerobic ATP restores PCr, reloads myoglobin) and lactacid (regenerates NAD+, lactate->pyruvate->glucose->glycogen). Tension = force/load a fibre resists; 4 S's: stretch, stimulation, size, stores. Length-tension: max tension at optimal resting sarcomere length ~2.0-2.3um (best filament overlap/cross-bridges); too short or too long lowers tension. Structural proteins: nebulin aligns/stabilises actin (Z disc along actin); titin stabilises myosin + elasticity + longitudinal force transfer (Z disc to M line); dystrophin anchors sarcomere to sarcolemma via beta-actin, lateral force transfer. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: no functional dystrophin (X-linked recessive, ~1 in 5000 male births) -> destabilised sarcolemma, fragile fibres rupture, inflammation/scarring, weakness, Duchenne gait, reduced cardiorespiratory function. Motor unit = one motor neuron + all fibres it innervates; grade tension by recruiting more/larger units and firing faster. Twitch = one excitation-contraction-relaxation; treppe (staircase) = rising early-twitch tension (delayed Ca re-uptake); wave summation = tension adds when the fibre can't fully relax; tetanus = fused twitches (unfused with slight relaxation, then complete smooth maximum); fatigue drops tension despite stimuli. Underlying cause: cytoplasmic Ca stays elevated so cross-bridges keep cycling. Muscle tone = resting tension from low-frequency twitches (posture); hypotonia/flaccidity (lower MND/ALS, myasthenia gravis, DMD), hypertonia/spasticity (upper MND, tetanus), prolonged hypertonia -> contracture. Motor neuron disease: degeneration of neurons controlling muscle; ALS affects upper + lower; atrophy, weakness. Isometric = constant length (hold), some cross-bridges, elastic proteins stretch to compensate; isotonic = constant tension (move) — concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens. Fibre types: Type I slow oxidative (red, high myoglobin/mitochondria/capillaries, fatigue-resistant, recruited first, endurance/posture); Type IIa fast oxidative-glycolytic (red-pink, intermediate); Type IIb fast glycolytic (white, few mitochondria, high glycogen, fatigable, recruited last, powerful bursts). Colour/capillaries/fatigue follow the fuel. Proportion mainly genetic (nature = sport suitability); training shifts it up to ~10% and increases diameter; diet (carbs) boosts glycogen. Exercise -> hypertrophy = more myofibrils per fibre (not more fibres) + more PCr/glycogen/triglyceride/mitochondrial enzymes. Progressive-overload strength training raises muscle strength (fewer back injuries), bone strength (less osteoporosis) and BMR (less weight gain); optimal ~6 near-maximal contractions x 3 sets, 3 days/week.

questions.question: Which enzyme carries the standing ATP cost of a muscle at rest?
questions.explanation: At rest the ongoing ATP cost is the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintaining the ion gradients action potentials spend. Ca²⁺-ATPase acts during relaxation, myosin ATPase during contraction, and creatine kinase banks phosphate as phosphocreatine.

questions.question: Relaxation of a muscle fibre is itself ATP-dependent because:
options: A. Creatine kinase must resynthesise phosphocreatine
B. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase must reset the resting membrane gradients
C. Myosin heads must actively push the filaments apart
D. The SR Ca²⁺-ATPase must pump calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Relaxation needs the SR Ca²⁺-ATPase to clear cytosolic calcium so cross-bridges detach. Myosin does not actively push (B); the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the resting cost (C); CK storage is a separate process (D).

questions.question: In the first seconds of a sprint, creatine kinase runs in the direction that:
options: A. Banks phosphate by moving it from ATP onto creatine
B. Converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺
C. Splits ATP to release the myosin cross-bridge
D. Regenerates ATP by moving phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP
questions.explanation: Creatine kinase is reversible: at rest it stores phosphate as phosphocreatine (B), but at the onset of activity it runs the other way, transferring that phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP almost instantly.

questions.question: Anaerobic glycolysis dominates a ~30-second maximal effort (once PCr runs low) mainly because it:
options: A. Draws on a steady oxygen supply from myoglobin
B. Delivers ATP faster than aerobic respiration, at the cost of total yield
C. Delivers twice the ATP per glucose that aerobic respiration does
D. Generates ATP more slowly but far more efficiently
questions.explanation: Glycolysis makes only 2 ATP per glucose (vs ~32 aerobically) but at a much higher rate — speed, not yield, is why it powers a ~30 s effort. C and D actually describe aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Aerobic respiration's trade-off against glycolysis is best summarised as:
options: A. Far more ATP per fuel molecule, and produced at a faster rate
B. The same ATP yield, but without requiring oxygen
C. Faster ATP, but obtainable only from fatty acids
D. Far more ATP per fuel molecule, but produced at a slower rate
questions.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation yields ~32 ATP per glucose — the most efficient system — but is rate-limited by oxygen supply, making it the slowest.

questions.question: When a muscle works beyond its oxygen supply, its pyruvate is:
options: A. Stored as phosphocreatine for later use
B. Converted to lactate, regenerating the NAD⁺ glycolysis needs to continue
C. Fully oxidised in the mitochondria to CO₂ and water
D. Converted directly into muscle glycogen
questions.explanation: Without enough O₂, pyruvate → lactate, which regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making ATP. Full oxidation (B) is the aerobic fate when O₂ is available.

questions.question: The 'accumulation' theory of muscle fatigue blames lost power on:
options: A. A fall in pH from lactate that impairs the ATPases and Ca²⁺–troponin binding
B. Exhaustion of the muscle's glycogen and oxygen stores
C. Degeneration of the motor neurons supplying the muscle
D. A rise in phosphocreatine that jams the cross-bridges
questions.explanation: Accumulation theory attributes fatigue to build-up — lactate lowering pH and disrupting CK, the ATPases and Ca²⁺ binding to troponin. Depletion of reserves (B) is the rival theory; C is motor neuron disease.

questions.question: Breathing stays elevated for minutes after a hard sprint in order to:
options: A. Build new muscle fibres to replace those damaged
B. Keep anaerobic glycolysis running at its peak rate
C. Repay an oxygen debt — restoring PCr and clearing lactate aerobically
D. Let the phosphagen system continue generating ATP
questions.explanation: The extra post-exercise O₂ (oxygen debt) rebuilds phosphocreatine, reloads myoglobin, and reconverts lactate → pyruvate → glycogen — all aerobic.

questions.question: Muscle tension refers to the:
options: A. Force a fibre can resist — the load it bears
B. Distance a fibre can shorten
C. Speed at which a fibre shortens
D. Frequency of its action potentials
questions.explanation: Tension is the force (load) a fibre resists; it depends on the four S's — stretch, stimulation, size and stores.

questions.question: At a sarcomere stretched well beyond its optimum, tension falls because:
options: A. The thick filaments crumple against the Z discs
B. Too few myosin heads still overlap actin to form cross-bridges
C. Calcium can no longer be released from the SR
D. The thin filaments overlap each other and obstruct the heads
questions.explanation: Over-stretch pulls the filaments apart, leaving too little overlap for cross-bridges. B and C describe the SHORT-sarcomere end; calcium release is unaffected by length (D).

questions.question: At a sarcomere compressed below its optimum, the main reason tension drops is that:
options: A. There is too little thin–thick overlap to form cross-bridges
B. Titin has been stretched past its elastic limit
C. Opposing thin filaments overlap and interfere with cross-bridge formation
D. There is not enough ATP for the power stroke
questions.explanation: Too short → thin filaments from opposite ends overlap (and thick filaments jam against the Z discs), fouling cross-bridges. Too LITTLE overlap (B) is the long-sarcomere end; length doesn't change ATP (D).

questions.question: Which structural protein anchors the sarcomere laterally to the sarcolemma?
questions.explanation: Dystrophin links the actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma — lateral force transfer. Titin runs Z-disc to M-line (longitudinal), nebulin aligns actin, and tropomyosin is a regulatory (not anchoring) protein.

questions.question: Titin is the sarcomere protein that:
options: A. Runs Z-disc to M-line, stabilising myosin and giving elasticity
B. Runs along actin from the Z disc, keeping the thin filament aligned
C. Forms the cross-bridge heads of the thick filament
D. Links the sarcomere to the sarcolemma for lateral force transfer
questions.explanation: Titin spans Z-disc to M-line — the molecular spring that stabilises myosin and provides passive elasticity. B is nebulin, C is dystrophin, D is myosin itself.

questions.question: Nebulin's role differs from titin's in that nebulin:
options: A. Aligns and stabilises the thin actin filament
B. Provides the sarcomere's passive elastic recoil
C. Anchors the fibre to the extracellular matrix
D. Sets the resting length of the thick filament
questions.explanation: Nebulin runs along actin, aligning the thin filament; titin gives the elasticity (B); dystrophin handles the anchoring to the matrix (C).

questions.question: In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, fibres are damaged because losing dystrophin:
options: A. Removes the sarcomere's elastic recoil, so it over-shortens
B. Blocks calcium release, so contractions become weak and brief
C. Leaves the sarcolemma unanchored and fragile, so it tears under normal contraction
D. Stops actin filaments being aligned, so cross-bridges misfire
questions.explanation: Without dystrophin the sarcolemma isn't tethered to the cytoskeleton, so it destabilises and fibres rupture with use. B and C describe titin/nebulin failures; calcium handling is not the primary defect (D).

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is inherited as:
options: A. A mitochondrial condition inherited down the maternal line
B. An autosomal dominant condition affecting both sexes equally
C. An X-linked dominant condition affecting mostly females
D. An X-linked recessive condition, so it mostly affects males
questions.explanation: DMD is X-linked recessive (~1 in 5000 live male births), from dystrophin-gene deletions.

questions.question: A single motor unit consists of:
options: A. All the fibres bundled in one fascicle
B. One muscle fibre and all the neurons that reach it
C. A group of sarcomeres within one fibre
D. One motor neuron and all the fibres its axon innervates
questions.explanation: A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all the fibres innervated by its axon branches — they contract together.

questions.question: A muscle grades its force from gentle to maximal mainly by:
options: A. Increasing the physical size of each fibre
B. Raising the resting cytosolic calcium level
C. Recruiting more and larger motor units and firing them faster
D. Lengthening each sarcomere toward its optimum
questions.explanation: Moment-to-moment force is graded by motor-unit recruitment (number and size) and firing rate; sarcomere length and fibre size are not rapid controls.

questions.question: Treppe (the staircase effect) is distinguished from wave summation because treppe is:
options: A. A climb in successive twitch tension at the START of stimulation, from lagging Ca²⁺ re-uptake
B. The fusion of twitches into one smooth maximal contraction
C. A partial adding of twitches that never fully relax
D. The fall in tension once the muscle begins to fatigue
questions.explanation: Treppe is the early warm-up rise in twitch tension, thought to reflect delayed SR calcium re-uptake. Summation (C) is incomplete relaxation adding tension; fusion (B) is tetanus.

questions.question: Wave summation raises tension because successive stimuli:
options: A. Each release progressively less calcium than the last
B. Arrive before the fibre has fully relaxed, so twitches add
C. Lengthen the sarcomere toward its optimum
D. Recruit additional motor units on every stimulus
questions.explanation: If a stimulus arrives before relaxation is complete, cytosolic calcium stays elevated and successive twitches sum onto one another.

questions.question: A fibre in complete tetanus holds maximal tension fundamentally because:
options: A. Each successive action potential is larger than the last
B. Cytosolic Ca²⁺ never falls, so cross-bridges keep cycling without relaxing
C. ATP supply rises to match the higher stimulus frequency
D. More motor units are recruited with every stimulus
questions.explanation: At high frequency the SR cannot clear calcium between stimuli, so calcium stays high and cross-bridges cycle continuously — a smooth fused maximum. Action potentials don't grow (B), and this is a single fibre's response (C).

questions.question: Resting muscle tone is produced by:
options: A. Low-frequency twitches giving a weak, sustained contraction
B. A sustained tetanic contraction of all motor units
C. The passive elasticity of titin alone
D. Steady maximal firing of the largest motor units
questions.explanation: Tone is the weak sustained contraction from low-frequency involuntary twitches (CNS + reflexes) that holds posture — neither tetanus nor purely passive.

questions.question: Spasticity (hypertonia) points to a lesion of the:
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron lesions (and tetanus) cause hypertonia/spasticity. Lower motor neuron loss, neuromuscular-junction disease (myasthenia gravis) and membrane disease (DMD) all cause hypotonia.

questions.question: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis causes muscle wasting because it:
options: A. Degenerates the upper and lower motor neurons driving the muscle
B. Removes dystrophin from the muscle membrane
C. Attacks the acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
D. Depletes the muscle's phosphocreatine stores
questions.explanation: ALS kills motor neurons (both upper and lower), cutting stimulation and causing atrophy. B is myasthenia gravis; C is DMD.

questions.question: Slowly lowering a heavy box to the floor is which kind of contraction?
options: A. Isotonic eccentric — the muscle lengthens under tension
B. A passive stretch with no active contraction
C. Isotonic concentric — the muscle shortens under tension
D. Isometric — the muscle length does not change
questions.explanation: Controlled lowering is an eccentric (lengthening) isotonic contraction. Shortening to lift is concentric; holding steady is isometric.

questions.question: In a true isometric contraction, cross-bridges still cycle yet whole-muscle length is unchanged because:
options: A. No cross-bridges actually form during the effort
B. The series-elastic elements stretch by exactly what the sarcomeres shorten
C. Calcium is not released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
D. The sarcomeres lengthen to compensate for the pull
questions.explanation: The sarcomeres do shorten internally, but the elastic elements (titin/tendon) stretch to absorb it, so overall length stays constant.

questions.question: Compared with a Type I fibre, a Type IIb (fast glycolytic) fibre has:
options: A. More myoglobin, which makes it appear redder
B. The same fatigue resistance but a faster contraction
C. More mitochondria but a lower glycogen store
D. Fewer mitochondria and capillaries, and less myoglobin
questions.explanation: Type IIb runs anaerobically — few mitochondria/capillaries, low myoglobin (pale), high glycogen, fast but fatigable. Type I is the mitochondria- and myoglobin-rich, red, fatigue-resistant fibre.

questions.question: Type I fibres appear red chiefly because they are rich in:
options: A. Glycogen granules stored for anaerobic glycolysis
B. Myofibrils packed tightly for maximal force
C. Sarcoplasmic reticulum for rapid calcium release
D. Myoglobin, matched by dense capillaries for aerobic metabolism
questions.explanation: Red colour comes from abundant myoglobin (with dense capillaries and mitochondria), all serving aerobic respiration. Glycogen is the pale IIb store; myofibril packing and SR relate to force and speed, not colour.

questions.question: As an effort becomes gradually harder, the fibre types are recruited in the order:
options: A. Type IIb, then Type IIa, then Type I
B. Type I, then Type IIa, then Type IIb
C. All three types together from the outset
D. Type IIa, then Type I, then Type IIb
questions.explanation: The slow, fatigue-resistant Type I fibres are recruited first and the fast, fatigable Type IIb last — the size principle.

questions.question: A person's ratio of fast- to slow-twitch fibres is:
options: A. Set mainly by diet and carbohydrate intake
B. Determined almost entirely by the type of training done
C. Fixed at birth and completely unchangeable
D. Largely set by genetics, with training shifting it by only ~10%
questions.explanation: Fibre-type ratio is mostly genetic (nature = suitability for a sport); training can shift it by up to ~10% and increase fibre diameter (nurture = performance).

questions.question: Progressive-overload strength training enlarges a muscle by:
options: A. Adding myofibrils within existing fibres, not adding new fibres
B. Increasing the total number of muscle fibres
D. Converting Type I fibres into Type IIb fibres
questions.explanation: Hypertrophy packs more myofibrils into existing fibres (plus more PCr, glycogen and mitochondrial enzymes) — it is not hyperplasia (new fibres).

pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.title: MEDI2004 W4 · Pharmacodynamics — Drug Action & Quantification
pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.content: Pharmacodynamics (L7 + L8). Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug; pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body and how (mechanism of action). PD studies how a drug binding its target produces a physiological response, so know the targets. Most targets are proteins; drugs activate, block/inhibit or modulate them. Four main protein targets: receptors, ion channels, enzymes, transporters (RITE). Receptors: agonist triggers transduction (ion-channel opening, enzyme change, DNA transcription), antagonist blocks endogenous mediators. Ion channels: blockers stop permeation, modulators change opening probability. Enzymes: inhibitors block the reaction, false substrates make abnormal metabolites, prodrugs are activated. Transporters: inhibitors block transport. Drugs also bind acceptors (e.g. plasma proteins) with no direct response. Specificity = one target, one site, one effect (ideal, reciprocal, never complete). Selectivity = preference for a target in particular cells/tissues; non-selective drug acts on >1 target at therapeutic dose (propranolol = non-selective beta-blocker). Affinity = tendency/strength of reversible drug-receptor binding, set by chemical structure; measured by dissociation constant KD = concentration occupying 50% of receptors; lower KD = higher affinity. Occupation governed by affinity; activation (AR -> AR*) governed by efficacy. Efficacy = capacity to activate a receptor and generate a response (Emax = maximal response, the curve height). Potency = mixed function of affinity + efficacy (EC50 = concentration for 50% maximal response, the curve position); lower potency = higher dose needed. On a concentration-response curve (CRC): full agonist reaches Emax; partial agonist plateaus below Emax even at full occupancy (lower efficacy); antagonist is flat (affinity, zero efficacy). Opioid example: enkephalin most potent + full efficacy, morphine less potent, buprenorphine partial agonist (~55% Emax). Constitutive activity = receptor active without ligand (Ri inactive <-> Ra active); inverse agonist has negative efficacy, stabilises Ri, lowers response below baseline. Competitive antagonist binds the same (orthosteric) site reversibly, zero efficacy, shifts the agonist CRC right WITHOUT changing slope or Emax = surmountable (more agonist overcomes). Irreversible antagonist forms covalent bonds, dissociates very slowly/never (e.g. aspirin acetylating COX), shifts right AND lowers slope/Emax = insurmountable. Receptor reserve (spare receptors): full response without full occupancy, so a CRC cannot be used to calculate affinity when spare receptors exist. Allosteric modulator binds a site distinct from the agonist's orthosteric site and increases (positive) or decreases (negative) the agonist's effect; benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the GABA-A receptor (enhance GABA-gated Cl- influx). Naloxone = competitive antagonist reversing opioids.

questions.question: Pharmacodynamics is the study of:
options: A. How the body absorbs, distributes and eliminates a drug
B. What the drug does to the body and how it does it
C. How a drug is metabolised by the liver
D. How a drug is excreted by the kidney
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (mechanism of action). Pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug.

questions.question: Most drug targets are:
questions.explanation: Most drug targets are proteins — a number likely to grow with gene therapy.

questions.question: The four main protein drug targets are:
options: A. Receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters
B. Receptors, lipids, DNA and enzymes
C. Agonists, antagonists, modulators and inhibitors
D. Carriers, cofactors, ligands and channels
questions.explanation: The four main protein targets are receptors, ion channels, enzymes and transporters (carriers) — remember 'RITE'.

questions.question: A drug acting as a 'false substrate' for an enzyme:
options: B. Is processed into an abnormal metabolite
questions.explanation: A false substrate is handled by the enzyme but yields an abnormal metabolite (as opposed to an inhibitor, which blocks the normal reaction).

questions.question: An ion-channel MODULATOR (as opposed to a blocker):
options: A. Physically plugs the pore to stop permeation
B. Increases or decreases the channel's opening probability
C. Forms a covalent bond with the channel
D. Is metabolised into an abnormal product
questions.explanation: Modulators change the opening probability of the channel; blockers stop permeation through the pore.

questions.question: An 'acceptor' differs from a receptor in that it:
options: A. Binds the drug but produces no direct functional response (e.g. plasma protein)
B. Always produces a stronger response
C. Is a type of enzyme
questions.explanation: Acceptors (e.g. plasma proteins) bind drug without generating a direct response, affecting distribution rather than action.

questions.question: Affinity is best defined as:
options: A. The tendency (strength) of a drug to bind its receptor
B. The capacity of a drug to activate a receptor
C. The maximal response a drug can produce
D. The dose needed for an effect
questions.explanation: Affinity is the tendency of a drug to bind its receptor — the strength of the reversible interaction, set by chemical structure.

questions.question: The dissociation constant KD is the concentration of drug that:
options: D. Produces 50% of the maximal response
questions.explanation: KD is the concentration occupying half the receptors — a binding (occupancy) measure, distinct from EC50 (a response measure).

questions.question: A drug with a LOWER KD has:
questions.explanation: A lower KD means less drug is needed to occupy half the receptors — i.e. higher affinity.

questions.question: The 'ideal' specific drug would:
options: A. Interact with one target at one site with one effect
B. Bind every receptor in the body
C. Have the highest possible potency
questions.explanation: Specificity is the ideal of one target, one site, one effect — it is reciprocal and never fully achieved in practice.

questions.question: Propranolol is described as:
questions.explanation: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker — it acts on more than one beta receptor at therapeutic concentration.

questions.question: Selectivity refers to a drug's:
options: A. Ability to bind only one target for its entire lifetime
B. Preference for a molecular target in particular cells or tissues
questions.explanation: Selectivity is a preference for a target in particular cells/tissues; a non-selective drug hits more than one target at therapeutic doses.

questions.question: A drug with high affinity but ZERO efficacy is:
questions.explanation: An antagonist binds well (affinity) but cannot activate the receptor (zero efficacy), so it produces no response of its own.

questions.question: Efficacy is:
options: A. The capacity of a drug to activate a receptor and generate a response
B. The tendency of a drug to bind a receptor
C. The dose needed to produce an effect
questions.explanation: Efficacy is the capacity to activate a receptor and produce a response — measured by Emax.

questions.question: On a concentration-response curve, Emax measures:
questions.explanation: Emax is the maximal response a drug can produce — the curve's height — a measure of efficacy.

questions.question: EC50 is:
options: A. The concentration producing 50% of the maximal response (a measure of potency)
C. The concentration occupying 50% of receptors
D. A measure of efficacy only
questions.explanation: EC50 is the concentration giving 50% of maximal response — the curve's horizontal position, a measure of potency.

questions.question: Receptor occupation is governed by affinity; activation (AR → AR*) is governed by:
questions.explanation: Occupation depends on affinity; whether the occupied receptor becomes active (AR*) depends on efficacy.

questions.question: Compared with a full agonist, a partial agonist:
options: A. Reaches a lower Emax even at full receptor occupancy
C. Produces no response at all
questions.explanation: A partial agonist has lower efficacy, so it plateaus below the full Emax even when all receptors are occupied.

questions.question: Saying drug X is 'more potent' than drug Y means:
options: A. X's curve sits further left (lower EC50) — it says nothing about Emax
B. X has a higher maximal effect
D. X is necessarily a full agonist
questions.explanation: Potency is horizontal position (EC50). More potent just means less drug is needed; the maximal effect (efficacy/Emax) is a separate axis.

questions.question: An inverse agonist:
options: A. Has zero efficacy like a competitive antagonist
B. Has negative efficacy, reducing constitutive activity below baseline
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists have negative efficacy — they stabilise the inactive receptor and lower the constitutive (baseline) response.

questions.question: Constitutive activity means a receptor:
options: A. Is active only when an agonist is bound
B. Is active even without a ligand (Ri ⇌ Ra equilibrium)
questions.explanation: Some receptors idle in an active state without ligand — an equilibrium between inactive (Ri) and active (Ra) — which inverse agonists can turn down.

questions.question: On the opioid concentration-response curves, buprenorphine behaves as:
options: C. A partial agonist (plateaus well below maximum)
questions.explanation: Buprenorphine plateaus around ~55% of maximum — a partial agonist, giving it a useful ceiling effect.

questions.question: An antagonist is characterised by:
options: C. Both high affinity and high efficacy
questions.explanation: Antagonists bind (affinity) but do not activate (zero efficacy), blocking the receptor.

questions.question: A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist concentration-response curve:
options: A. To the right, with Emax unchanged
B. To the right, with a reduced Emax
questions.explanation: Competitive antagonism produces a parallel right-shift without changing the slope or Emax — it is surmountable.

questions.question: Competitive antagonism is 'surmountable' because:
options: A. Adding more agonist can overcome it (same site, reversible)
questions.explanation: Because the block is reversible and at the same site, enough extra agonist out-competes it, restoring the full response.

questions.question: An irreversible antagonist affects the curve by:
options: A. Shifting it right AND reducing the slope/Emax
B. Shifting it right with no change in Emax
questions.explanation: Irreversible (covalent) block removes receptors permanently, shifting the curve right and lowering Emax — insurmountable.

questions.question: A clinical example of an irreversible antagonist is:
questions.explanation: Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly — a rare clinically used irreversible antagonist; its effect lasts the platelet's lifetime.

questions.question: Receptor reserve ('spare receptors') means that:
options: A. A full response can occur without full occupancy, so a CRC can't give affinity
B. There are no receptors present
C. More drug is always required
questions.explanation: With spare receptors a maximal response is reached before all receptors are occupied, so the CRC cannot be used to calculate affinity.

questions.question: An allosteric modulator binds:
options: A. A site distinct from the agonist's (orthosteric) site
B. The same site as the agonist
C. Only the enzyme active site
questions.explanation: Allosteric modulators bind a separate site and increase (positive) or decrease (negative) the agonist's effect — unlike competitive drugs at the orthosteric site.

questions.question: Benzodiazepines act on the GABA_A receptor as:
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators — they don't open the channel themselves but enhance GABA's effect.

questions.question: Naloxone reverses an opioid overdose by acting as a:
options: A. Competitive antagonist at the opioid receptor
questions.explanation: Naloxone competitively (reversibly) out-competes the opioid at the receptor — a surmountable, competitive antagonist.

hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.title: MHHS2401 W4 · Anatomy of the Hand
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.content: Anatomy of the hand (Dr Strkalj). Skeleton: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals (I-V from thumb), 14 phalanges (thumb has proximal + distal only, no middle). Carpals proximal row radial->ulnar: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ('Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle'). Carpals not visible at birth; capitate ossifies first (1-3 months) then anticlockwise. Carpal bones form a bony arch closed by the flexor retinaculum = carpal tunnel; contents = 9 tendons + median nerve (4 flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 flexor digitorum profundus, 1 flexor pollicis longus tendon + median nerve). Ulnar nerve and extensor tendons lie OUTSIDE the tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome = median nerve compression. Scaphoid is the most fractured carpal (risk of avascular necrosis). Joints: wrist (radiocarpal) = condyloid synovial (distal radius + articular disc / proximal carpal row EXCEPT pisiform); movements flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction. Intercarpal = plane (gliding); midcarpal (between rows) aids extension/abduction. Carpometacarpal (CMC) joints of medial 4 = plane; thumb CMC = SADDLE synovial joint (trapezium + base of 1st metacarpal) giving opposition. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) of medial 4 = condyloid (flex/ext/abd/add) with collateral ligaments, palmar ligament, deep transverse metacarpal ligaments (tie metacarpal heads 2-5). Interphalangeal (IP) = hinge (flexion/extension). Rheumatoid arthritis = chronic autoimmune disease of synovial joints (~1 in 50 Australians, women>men), small joints of hand/feet, MCP ulnar deviation + erosion. Muscles: extrinsic (forearm bellies, long tendons) - anterior superficial (pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU), intermediate (FDS), deep (FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus); posterior superficial (ECRL, ECRB, ED, EDM, ECU), deep (supinator, APL, EPB, EPL, EI). Intrinsic: thenar (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), hypothenar (abductor/flexor/opponens digiti minimi), adductor pollicis, 4 lumbricals, 4 dorsal + 3 palmar interossei, palmaris brevis. Innervation: ULNAR nerve supplies all intrinsics EXCEPT thenar muscles and lateral 2 lumbricals (median). Median = 'MEat LOAF' (Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis). Dorsal interossei ABduct = DAB (from adjacent metacarpal shafts, insert extensor hood + base proximal phalanx of index/middle/ring); palmar interossei ADduct = PAD. First dorsal interosseous is pierced by the radial artery. Lumbricals arise from FDP tendons, insert extensor hoods, flex MCP + extend IP. Ulnar nerve lesion = claw hand (worst ring/little fingers); median lesion = thenar wasting/ape hand.
